planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Ochlockonee is a low-chill (about 400-450 hours), late-ripening rabbiteye that extends the harvest season and needs another rabbiteye cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist through the long southern summer. Ochlockonee is a University of Florida-released rabbiteye blueberry named for the Ochlockonee River in the Florida Panhandle, valued for ripening late in the season, after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, which lets home growers stretch fresh blueberry harvest into July. The vigorous, upright bush produces firm, medium-to-large, good-flavored berries in heavy clusters, and its low chill requirement makes it well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South. Fertilize lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest, and remove old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing vigorous fruiting wood.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Cultivars
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Blueberry Variety Profiles
Ison's Nursery and Vineyard variety notes

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Vernon ripens mid-season and needs another rabbiteye cultivar such as Climax or Tifblue nearby for cross-pollination and full fruit set.

directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Vernon is a mid-season rabbiteye blueberry bred for the Gulf South, producing an upright, vigorous, productive bush with firm, well-flavored, medium-to-large berries that hold well on the bush without excessive splitting in humid weather. It fills the harvest gap between early cultivars like Climax and later ones like Tifblue or Ochlockonee, giving home orchards a steadier, more extended supply of fresh fruit. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid high-nitrogen feeding late in the season, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Varieties
Mississippi State University Extension — Blueberry Production Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Beckyblue has a low chill requirement (around 350-400 hours), ripens early, and needs another low-chill rabbiteye such as Climax nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, in full sun with a compatible early-season pollinator nearby. Beckyblue is a University of Florida-released rabbiteye blueberry bred specifically for the low winter chill of the Deep South and Florida, ripening among the earliest of the rabbiteye cultivars and giving Gulf Coast growers a jump on the blueberry season. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and pleasantly mild-flavored, borne on a vigorous, spreading bush. Because it flowers early, plant it in a site with reasonable air drainage to reduce frost risk to the blooms in years with a late cold snap. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, mulch well to conserve moisture, and prune out old wood each winter to sustain strong early yields.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Cultivars
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Blueberry Variety Profiles
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Blueberry Production

common_name: Lane Muscadine Grape (Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine)

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Lane is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) black muscadine released by the University of Georgia and does not require a separate pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis and prune heavily each winter.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Lane is a modern University of Georgia muscadine release valued for its very large, glossy black berries with a thinner, more tender skin than many older black muscadines, along with sweet, richly flavored flesh well suited to fresh eating. The self-fertile vine is vigorous and productive, ripening in the mid-to-late season, and its improved skin quality and berry size have made it a popular choice for both home gardens and u-pick plantings across the Gulf South. Keep vines well watered during fruit development for the best berry size, and thin overcrowded shoots in summer to improve air circulation and reduce fruit rot in humid weather.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Home Gardens
North Carolina State University Extension — Muscadine Grape Cultivar Guide

common_name: Sweet Jenny Muscadine Grape (Very Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine)

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Sweet Jenny is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) black muscadine released by the University of Georgia breeding program and does not require a separate pollinator vine.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Sweet Jenny is a University of Georgia muscadine release notable for producing some of the largest fruit of any black muscadine cultivar, with sweet, mild-flavored flesh and a skin tender enough for easy fresh eating rather than just juice or wine. The self-fertile vine is vigorous, productive, and ripens over an extended mid-to-late season window, making it a favorite for home gardeners who want big, showy fruit without needing a second pollinator vine. Water consistently during fruit sizing for the largest berries, and thin crowded shoots in summer to improve air circulation and reduce fruit rot in humid Gulf South conditions.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Home Gardens
North Carolina State University Extension — Muscadine Grape Cultivar Guide
